Beyond the kernel, August brought a noticeable wave of core-stack bumps and a refresh of the NVIDIA driver stack.

Things worth your attention

Kernel jump to 7.2.2

The kernel package was built for Arch on August 28, with matching headers and documentation. Last month’s ISO still shipped 7.1.5, so the 7.2 promotion is the change users will notice first. Linux 7.2 itself was released on schedule around mid-August, after a busy cycle. The big-ticket items were Cache Aware Scheduling, partial Apple M3 support, USB4STREAM support, AMDGPU HDMI 2.1 FRL, Btrfs large folios enabled by default, removal of the legacy strncpy() API from the kernel, and the start of the AF_ALG deprecation. The DRM “fair” scheduler policy that was originally supposed to become the default in 7.2 was reverted at the last minute to FIFO after a regression report, so 7.2.2 ships with FIFO as the default.

Core stack refresh

GCC moved to the 16.2.1 series, glibc to 2.44, Python to 3.14.7, and mkinitcpio to 41.1. OpenSSH is at 10.5p1, OpenSSL at 3.6.4, and iproute2 at 7.2.0. The August 10 Linux firmware bundle is in place, covering AMD, Intel, NVIDIA, Realtek, Qualcomm, Broadcom, MediaTek, and the usual long tail.

Graphics got a substantial refresh too: Mesa moved to 26.2.1, and the Vulkan drivers for AMD, Intel, Nouveau, Panfrost, and Freedreno all rebuilt against it.

NVIDIA stack on 610.57.04

August brought the NVIDIA 610.57.04 driver to the repositories. The packages now shipping include nvidia-open 610.57.04-11, nvidia-open-dkms 610.57.04-1, nvidia-open-lts 610.57.04-9, plus nvidia-utils, nvidia-settings, and opencl-nvidia at 610.57.04. If you are on the Open Kernel Modules path, this is the snapshot you want.

Networking and base utilities

NetworkManager is at 1.58.1, which landed in August with WPA3, DNS, and modem fixes. arch-install-scripts updated to 31.2. Archinstall itself did not get a new release in this window, and Archiso is unchanged from last month.

Desktop environments

KDE Plasma moved to 6.7.4 in the repos, with KDE Frameworks packages now on the 6.29 series. GNOME Shell is at 50.4. COSMIC Desktop 1.7 arrived in August, covering the compositor, panel, launcher, settings, file manager, terminal, software store, workspaces, and the rest of the stack.

Applications

LibreOffice moved to 26.8, Firefox to 154, Chromium to 152, and Vivaldi to 8.1. QEMU is at 11.1, libvirt at 12.6, and VirtualBox at 7.2.16. The container stack moved on too: Docker 29.7.2, Docker Compose 5.5, containerd 2.3.4, and Podman 6.1.

Smaller changes

Networking utilities

iproute2 is at 7.2.0, and the NetworkManager bump carries the usual batch of small fixes around WPA3 handshakes, DNS resolver ordering, and modem state transitions.

Build chain

GCC 16.2.1 is the headline compiler change. Combined with glibc 2.44 and binutils tracking current, expect rebuilt ports across the system. Anyone building packages against extra will see a cascade of rebuilds in the next couple of weeks.

Repository health reminder

If you pull from the AUR, this is a good moment to review your PKGBUILDs. The malicious adoptions incident from late June is still fresh, and a high volume of malicious adoptions and updates were detected around that window. Don’t trust the latest version of an AUR package by version number alone.

Bug fixes

NVIDIA 610.57.04 fixes a long list of Vulkan gaming and kernel-mode issues that piled up against 590.x. NetworkManager 1.58.1 carries WPA3 negotiation fixes and a modem-manager path that handled a few edge cases poorly. Plasma 6.7.4 fixes KWin, Discover, and login-manager bugs. LibreOffice 26.8 ships its usual paragraph-composer and variable-font fixes. Per-package Arch bug reports track the rest.

Sources

Official release details on the Arch release engineering page for 2026.09.01 with SHA256, BLAKE2b, and the PGP fingerprint for verification. The Arch release list confirms kernel 7.2.2 on this snapshot. Coverage from Linuxiac on the September 2026 ISO and LinuxCompatible on the 1.5 GB release. Linux kernel version history on Wikipedia for the 7.2 release date and prominent features. Phoronix coverage of Linux 7.2 for the DRM scheduler revert and broader cycle detail.

item.title: Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS: what the first point release actually fixes
item.description: Resolute Raccoon's first point release shipped on August 27 with refreshed ISOs, a stack of desktop and kernel fixes, and security updates through August 25. No new HWE stack, that waits for 26.04.2.
item.content:encoded:
Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, the first point release of Resolute Raccoon, landed on August 27. The official announcement is on the Ubuntu Discourse and the detailed per-package changelog lives on documentation.ubuntu.com. If you have been running 26.04 since April, you already have most of this through the archive. The point release matters most for fresh installs and for anyone upgrading from 24.04.

There is no new Hardware Enablement stack in 26.04.1. Canonical has held that back for 26.04.2, which will follow the 26.10 release. So 26.04.1 still ships the original 26.04 kernel and graphics stack, just with everything that has landed in the archive since the initial release rolled up into refreshed installation media.

Things worth your attention

Installation media

Several fixes went into livecd-rootfs. RISC-V no longer forces earlycon=sbi and uses the generic kernel flavour on desktop images instead of HWE. The nocloud data format was corrected, and kernel plus initrd now ship in the casper directory with mode 0644, which fixes a netboot tarball that previously arrived with a kernel readable only by root. If you have been building PXE or netboot images for arm or riscv hardware, that last one is the kind of bug you would have hit immediately and then spent an hour debugging.

Upgrade path from 24.04

ubuntu-release-upgrader had a few quirks smoothed out. DistUpgradeQuirks formatting and linting now pass cleanly. The Noble-to-resolute path is now marked Prompt=lts. On Raspberry Pi installs the upgrader forces piboot-try over flash-kernel. The mirror list was refreshed in both ubuntu-release-upgrader and python-apt.

Canonical will not offer the automatic 24.04 to 26.04.1 upgrade for a couple of weeks, while a planned backport addresses regressions in a recent rust-coreutils. If you do not want to wait, do-release-upgrade -d works right now.

Desktop fixes

The bulk of the work is in the desktop. Mutter got a series of Ubuntu patches: it no longer processes other events while waiting for a snap id during window creation (a synchronous operation that should not have been re-entrant), fixes a cursor that kept spinning after launching an app, fixes the cursor not changing inside popups, acknowledges snaps that ship non-desktop CLI apps, cherry-picks the upstream fix for a crash on hot-plugging similar monitors, and fixes a gdctl crash on invalid backlight values. The same-window drag and drop on touchscreens is repaired.

GNOME Shell picked up a fix for accidentally removing search providers when one was unregistered, a patch to load the Ubuntu logo image synchronously so the first frame of the login screen is the real one, and the dash no longer notifies the a11y layer twice per icon. Nautilus restores the progress bar indicator that had been showing zero progress, fixes a crash when opening bookmarks from the dock, restores the previous default action in the “permanently delete” confirmation dialog, and gets the fallback icon sizing back in sync with the zoom level. GNOME Control Center no longer resets the autostart toggle when you change apps. GDM fixes the wrong XDG_SESSION_TYPE for X11 sessions. gnome-initial-setup now has translatable release-notes copy and pulls in updated translations from Launchpad.

Several GNOME stack components moved to newer upstream bugfix releases: gtk4, libadwaita-1, gnome-session, gnome-text-editor, gdm3, nautilus, gnome-remote-desktop, papers, orca, and at-spi2-core. LibreOffice moved to a new upstream release twice. WSL setup syncs the terminal profile with the desktop theme. Ubuntu’s resources library now reads localized app names from langpacks, which fixes the English-only app names that showed up in the desktop search for many deb-installed apps. cups-filters no longer loads parport_pc unconditionally, fixing a boot hang on machines without a parallel port.

Fingerprint readers and biometrics

libfprint gained a new driver for the Egis ETU905 fingerprint reader, and the Goodix MoC driver no longer reports inconsistent enrollment progress when you swipe quickly.

Security updates in the archive

Several notable security items are bundled in. PackageKit had a TOCTOU race on transaction flags. Exim4 got two security updates: a one-byte write into a freed buffer, and an information disclosure in PROXYv2. Rsync carried a security regression fix from the May 2026 update. OpenSSL picked up a fix for the HollowByte denial-of-service issue. apparmor received a new upstream release as an SRU backport. systemd fixed the cloud-init delay caused by the systemd-networkd resolve hook. The full list of Ubuntu Security Notices through August 25, 2026 is included.

Smaller changes

Server, cloud, and virt

Libvirt fixes excessive memory allocation when physical_package_id is large and a logic bug that hurt performance for some interface types with ingress-only QoS rules. QEMU gets a fix for a virgl crash from an unset memory region, an early-stop fix for the module loading function, loads the kvm module for riscv64, makes the Zicbop extension available in RISC-V KVM VMs, and fixes a race with iothreads and throttle groups. cloud-init cherry-picks the iBFT-based iSCSI root detection for Oracle dracut images. resource-agents now stops the fsidd daemon before stopping nfs-server. Heat preserves auto-populated binding:profile fields during updates. byobu no longer writes the prompt runtime to stderr.

Kernel and hardware

Linux moved to 7.0.0-15.15 across the board. linux-raspi moved to 7.0.0-1010.10. linux-nvidia moved to 7.0.0-1006.6. The intel-ipu7 and intel-ipu7-isys modules were being shipped unsigned, which broke Secure Boot on systems that rely on them, and that is now fixed. Qualcomm X1E laptops were triggering hardware protection shutdowns from speaker overdrive, also fixed. nvidia-graphics-drivers-580 moved to 580.159.03 and fixes a suspend crash caused by a missing objtool jump_label NOP conversion. Canonical Kmod keys rotated to the 2025 set. libinput gained a quirk for the Synaptic 06CB:D024 touchpad found on HP haptic touchpads. webkit2gtk works on arm64 with 64KB page sizes. flash-kernel knows about the SpacemiT K3 CoM260 IFX board. ubuntu-raspi-settings lowers the zstd and xz compression levels to avoid OOM on memory-constrained boards and disables the tmpfs /tmp mount on systems with low RAM.

Foundations

systemd fixed the postinst order so rsyslog’s tmpfiles config is honored during upgrade, skips two flaky upstream tests on the build, and stops opening the netfilter socket on every system. debootstrap detects SHA512 in Release index files. grub-initrd-fallback.service now runs after grub2-common.service. distro-info-data records that the Ubuntu Legacy Support extension is now 15 years. tzdata updated to the current release.

Metapackage churn

The desktop metapackages now recommend gst-audio-thumbnailer and gst-video-thumbnailer. pollinate was removed from cloud-minimal, server, server-minimal, and server-raspi, and curl was added back to cloud-minimal and server-minimal to replace what had been pulled in implicitly by pollinate.

Bug fixes worth knowing about

A few items are worth flagging even if they are not headline features. software-properties crashed on Python 3.14 forkserver multiprocessing during driver detection and crashed on a typo in the section name check for manually installed drivers; both are fixed. libpciaccess pointed pc.ids at the wrong path. apport now handles zstd-compressed coredumps, retraces correctly behind an HTTP proxy, and no longer adds a stray .txt extension to retrace artifacts. update-notifier always shows a notification if one is requested. freerdp3 had a clipboard regression from a prior security update and is back. Remmina fixed pre- and post-connect command handling. systemd-tmpfiles runs after debhelper so rsyslog’s config is no longer dropped during an upgrade.

The AppArmor profile set picked up fixes for transmission-gtk, uucore locale reads, lsusb uevent file reads, and alsamixer asound config reads.

Sources

Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS release announcement on the Ubuntu Community Discourse. Changes in Ubuntu 26.04.1 on documentation.ubuntu.com, with per-package bugs and Launchpad links. Resolute Raccoon release schedule for the 26.04.2 timeline. Phoronix coverage for the “no new HWE” detail. 9to5Linux announcement. Ubuntu Security Notices for Resolute.

item.title: KDE Plasma 6.8 freeze: what is already locked in
item.description: Soft feature freeze landed August 27, 2026. Plasma 6.8 branches from there, two betas follow, and the final release is due October 14. Here is what is settled so far, sorted into the sections you can read.
item.content:encoded:
KDE Plasma 6.8 hit its soft feature freeze on August 27. That is when the 6.7.80 tag branched off and the 6.8 milestone stopped taking features. Two public betas come next: 6.7.90 on September 10 and 6.7.91 on September 24. The stable release is due October 14, 2026.

Beta 1 has not shipped yet, so everything below landed before the freeze. Bug-fix batches arrive with the betas. The 6.8 branch no longer accepts new features.

Things worth your attention

Wayland is the only session now

Plasma 6.8 removes the X11 session. The login screen no longer lists it as an option. KDE announced this direction in November 2025 (“Going all-in on a Wayland future”); 6.8 is the release that actually deletes the fallback. If you still run X11-only software, this is the cycle to make a plan. It affects everyone on X11 and the few tools that expect an X server.

NVIDIA triple buffering on by default

KWin now turns on triple buffering for NVIDIA GPUs by default. The option stayed disabled for a long time because of earlier bug reports, but the code is now stable enough to ship. NVIDIA users should see less stutter in windowed and full-screen use without touching settings. The work underneath is the dynamic triple buffering support that landed in Plasma 6.1 and had been off by default since.

Client-side decorations get shadows and rounding

KWin now draws a shadow, outline, and rounded corners on CSD (client-side-decorated) windows that do not ship their own. A “This Week in Plasma” post from July 18, 2026 (“Shadows for Steam and Discord”) covers the KWin commit. It matters for Steam, Discord, and other Electron or CSD apps, whose square corners now match the rest of the desktop.

Multi-monitor identification

Plasma 6.8 puts a color-coded number badge on each monitor wherever you set up displays. With two identical panels next to each other, the badge tells you which is which. Adjusting brightness on an external monitor is also faster. This helps anyone running more than one screen, especially with duplicate models.

Spectacle records audio

Spectacle can now capture system or microphone audio during a screen recording, not only the video. That closes a gap the built-in tool had next to standalone recorders. Anyone who records their screen and wants narration or system sound in the file gets it now.

Smaller changes

System Settings

  • Wi-Fi access points can pick a channel automatically on the Networks page.
  • Plasma Login Manager now handles distros with older systemd versions, such as KDE neon.

Theming and integration

  • Dark GTK 2 themes are detected better, and a matching icon theme is applied on its own.
  • Peek at Desktop and Window Aperture effects now follow the system-wide animation speed setting.

Apps

  • Emoji Selector moves to Unicode 17, so it can insert emoji such as 🫪 (distorted face), 🫍 (orca), 🫈 (hairy creature), 🪊 (trombone), and 🛘 (landslide). The full Unicode 17 set also adds 🫯 (fight cloud), 🪎 (treasure chest), and 🧑‍🩰 (ballet dancer).
  • Plasma Browser Integration supports the Flatpak build of Microsoft Edge.
  • The lock screen tells you when the Slow Keys accessibility feature is on.
  • Low-battery notifications for connected devices now show during full-screen apps.
  • Wallpaper slideshows can be set to stay on one image.
  • Emulated Input reaches version 1.6 for better virtual keyboard, mouse, and touch handling.

Bug fixes

None published yet. Beta 1 and Beta 2 each bring their own fix batches; this section fills in once those NEWS files are out.

Still in flight

These are proposed or under review for 6.8 but were not merged as of freeze. They may slip to a later release:

  • More NVIDIA Vulkan and Wayland work tied to the 610 driver series.
  • Extra CSD polish past shadows (mentioned in planning, no merged MR at freeze time).
  • Refinements to the color-coded monitor badges, for example remembering per-connector choices.

Under the hood

Plasma 6.8 builds on Qt 6.11 and KDE Frameworks 6.30. The merged “noteworthy” merge requests for the 6.8 milestone are tracked on Invent, and the list grows through the beta window. MR numbers are not all public at freeze time, so this section expands when Beta 1 NEWS lands.

Sources

KDE Plasma 6 schedule and the 6.8 dependency stack (Qt 6.11, Frameworks 6.30) on the Plasma 6 page. 9to5Linux on what to expect in Plasma 6.8. KDE blog on going all-in on a Wayland future. “This Week in Plasma: Shadows for Steam and Discord” (July 18, 2026) covers the CSD shadow commit. Unicode 17 emoji additions on Emojipedia.

item.title: GNOME 51 “A Coruña”: what actually changed since GNOME 50
item.description: Alpha and beta are out, the final release lands September 16. Here is everything noteworthy, everything minor, and the bug fixes worth knowing about, sorted into sections you can actually read.
item.content:encoded:
As of late August 2026, GNOME 51 has an alpha (July 3) and a beta (August 15). The final release is due September 16. Beta also started the UI, feature, and API freezes, so this covers practically the whole release: fixes and translations will still land before the final, new features will not.

Things worth your attention

Graphics and the compositor

Mutter can now blur window backgrounds through a new Wayland protocol, ext-background-effect-v1, and GTK 4.23.3 added the client side (ext-background-effect). The compositor does the blurring rather than the app, so it works universally. Until now this was shim and extension territory.

Timing is the other big area. Michel Dänzer sent a series of frame scheduling patches to Mutter (Mutter MR 5138, Mutter MR 5131, Mutter MR 5183, Mutter MR 5167, Mutter MR 5156), and Benjamin Otte reworked the GTK frame clock: better prediction of when a frame will actually hit the screen, fewer dropped frames, and a fix for the frameclockidle deadlock. Animation and scrolling smoothness should improve across the board, most visibly at high refresh rates and on VRR displays.

Cursors can ship as SVG now, in a format compatible with KDE. Cursor theme authors no longer need to generate raster sets for every HiDPI scale.

Mutter fills in mastering display metadata for HDR output.

One breaking change: Mutter dropped legacy NVIDIA drivers (Mutter MR 5079). Old proprietary versions stop working; current NVIDIA and Open kernel modules are fine.

Shell and login

Web login and a unified auth mechanism (MR GNOME Shell MR 3212): the login screen can offer several authentication mechanisms side by side, including logging in through the web. This is the biggest GDM and Shell change in years.

Shell started honoring the reduced-motion setting (initial support), holding back motion animations for people who want less of them. GTK respects the same setting.

The COPY, CUT, and PASTE keys work in Shell text entries.

Calendar reminders pop up as Shell notifications (GNOME Shell MR 1064), so you no longer need to open the calendar app to see them. Monitor brightness is saved and restored across sessions, too.

The VA-API H.264 screencast pipeline gained rate control, so screen recording loads the machine less. The extensions app moved to its own repository. Extension authors should note that async disable() is explicitly disallowed now; until recently that path led straight to race conditions.

GDM has a fallback session setting (it kicks in when a user has no preferred session or theirs is unusable), an option to turn off the local greeter on headless machines, and KMSCON VT compatibility. Conflicting sessions are enumerated through logind, so GDM sees sessions started by ThinLinc or TigerVNC as well. XDG_DATA_DIRS no longer hard-codes /usr/share above /usr/local/share, which means hacking on a locally built gnome-shell no longer requires rebuilding GDM with the same prefix. The remote display D-Bus API and GDM settings finally have documentation.

What left the platform

Removed modules: gcr-3, gnome-keyring, evince (Papers replaces it), and gtksourceview-4. Together with oo7-portal from the API section, the direction for secret storage is clear: the oo7 stack. Distros can still package these themselves, but they are no longer part of the GNOME platform.

Smaller changes

Performance and internals

  • Nautilus: faster view reloading, blocking IO pushed off the main thread, no duplicated loading locations.
  • Software: faster icon loading and PackageKit repository refinement.
  • System Monitor: reworked cgroups performance.
  • tinysparql: faster ICU full-text tokenizer; localsearch refactored code shared between processes.
  • GtkSourceView: faster context engine and search context.
  • Shell screencasts minimize stage paints and buffer copies.
  • GLib: the GNetworkMonitor netlink backend behaves like iproute2 and pulls the route table less often.
  • libdex: reworked work stealing in the thread pool; idle workers sleep instead of scanning peers, and work distributes better.
  • GTK: GPU cache scaling limits, text view caches pixel height, motion history is always collected for input prediction.
  • Sysprof: libsysprof-capture optimizations.

Security

GLib’s GDBusServer suffered a pre-authentication DoS through unbounded SASL line buffering (GLib issue 3985).

Evolution Data Server got a hardening series: a shell command injection fix in NTLM SASL, ENVID sanitization against SMTP command injection, POP3 rejecting CRLF-bearing credentials (command injection), CardDAV validating photo/logo URI origins against SSRF, a MIME nesting depth limit against stack exhaustion, HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects rejected, and OAuth2 state parameters against CSRF.

gvfs hardened input validation across afp/dav/ftp/mtp/sftp backends, wipes passwords from memory before freeing them, and fixed crashes in the OneDrive, MTP, and SMB backends. glycin switched its sandbox seccomp policy from an allowlist to a blocklist, a sturdier second line of defense. Epiphany quotes command-line input before passing it to the shell (Epiphany MR 2094) and carries the memory-corruption and crash fixes above. dconf’s safe GVDB writer protects settings integrity on NFS.
